source.title: Proof Artifact Co-training for Theorem Proving with Language Models
source.authors: Jesse Michael Han; Jason M. Rute; Yu-Huai Wu; Edward W. Ayers; Stanislas Polu

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out theorem-proving success across model sizes, a different downstream measure from the original loss-scaling studies.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws as background but does not measure held-out text-pretraining loss, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its Figure 4 reports theorem-proving pass rates across three model sizes; those results bear on V6. Validation losses there are for the proof-artifact and tactic objectives, not held-out text-pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: Figure 4 compares theorem-proving pass rates for three model sizes (121M, 163M, 837M) in one PACT co-training setup. This is a downstream-performance-versus-scale result in a new setting (formal theorem proving in Lean), so it bears on V6. It does not measure held-out text-pretraining loss, fit power laws, extrapolate, or vary compute allocation, so V1–V4 and V7 are not tested. T3 fits better than the reader's T2, since the paper does not aim at the scaling-law question; size scaling is a side experiment.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors state performance is highly correlated with model size, with larger models generalizing better even in the overfitted regime, and leave multi-billion-parameter scaling to future work. The abstract's remark that data scarcity disrupts scaling with size is motivation citing Kaplan et al.; the paper does not test it directly.
record.recipe_differences: This is a theorem-proving evaluation across three parameter counts using a PACT co-training setup, not a held-out text-loss scaling-law experiment; it does not fit loss curves or vary training compute and tokens systematically.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning validation loss on the tactic objective falls with model size (1.23, 1.11, 0.91), and the mix1 loss falls too (0.13, 0.12, 0.09). Lower tactic loss accompanies higher pass rate across sizes and across training setups (Figure 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In fine-tuning on a downstream objective, lower fine-tuning validation loss tracks better downstream task success (not pretraining loss).

record.problems: The size comparison includes only three models and one training setup. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the pass rates and does not test multi-billion-parameter models.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results meet the row criteria for the claim versions: the paper's validation losses concern proof-artifact and tactic objectives, and other theorem-proving comparisons vary training data or procedure rather than test the specified loss-scaling versions.

untested.parts: Predictability: no fit or functional form, only three points, and no prediction of larger models. No link to pretraining loss is tested; the reported losses are fine-tuning validation losses. Only one downstream task and one training setup.
Entirely untested: no text-pretraining loss scaling.
Entirely untested: sizes differ in depth and width together, and parameter count is not held fixed.
No power-law fit to the fine-tuning validation losses. Only three sizes, with no functional form tested.

missing.what: Per-size validation losses on tactic/mix1/mix2 objectives (1.23/1.11/0.91 tactic). These would let a researcher relate fine-tuning loss to pass rate and see size scaling of fine-tuning loss.

record.verdict_notes: This is a weak V6 test: three sizes, one setup, a secondary experiment in a PACT methods paper. The 121M and 163M models share width (768) but differ in depth, and all three use different learning rates and token counts, so the size effect is not cleanly isolated. Test-set contamination checks (Appendix B.1) lower the best model's pass rate by about 1 point; this was not reported per size.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out text-pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law fits and the several-orders-of-magnitude range.
No fits on smaller runs or predictions of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token counts.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
No tests of power-law loss forms across modalities or the specified alternative training regimes.

Tests theorem-proving success only, in one PACT training setup and at three model sizes. It does not establish a predictive fit, test pretraining-loss-to-downstream-performance prediction, or assess other downstream tasks.
No investigation of scaling-law exponents, compute-optimal splits, fitting choices, or departures from power-law curves.

rows.subject: 121m model
rows.operation_detail: Compared theorem-proving performance across model sizes in the PACT training setup.
rows.locator: Figure 4; Section 4, Effect of Model Size
rows.note: Reported separately for this model size in the model-size comparison.
rows.check: Each row holds one model's pass rate. The V6 effect (rise with size) exists only across r1–r3, so r1 (121M, 35.1%) is the reference point rather than an effect on its own. Sizes are confounded with depth (6 vs 12 vs 24 layers), width (768 vs 1536), learning rate (0.0016 / 0.0014 / 0.00025) and tokens elapsed (82B / 80B / 71B). No uncertainty is given; pass rates are a 3-run average.

relationships.condition: PACT setup WebMath > mix1 + mix2 + tactic, 121M–837M parameters, 3071 held-out Lean theorems
relationships.reason: Pass rate rises monotonically with size, from 35.1% to 39.8% to 48.4% (r1–r3). The authors say performance is highly correlated with size. However, there are only three points, no fit, and size is confounded with depth, LR and tokens.
relationships.display_finding: Pass rates increased 35.1%→39.8%→48.4%, but the three-size comparison had no fitted curve and also varied depth, learning rate and training tokens.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
